newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan to crack down on official corruption.
newsitem.headline: Japan to crack down on official corruption.

text.p: Japan's government will crack down on official corruption following a series of bribery scandals that have brought down a deputy health minister and a prefectural governor, newspapers reported on Sunday.
The government will ban socialising with business contacts and draw up a bureaucratic code of conduct and appoint an ethics overseer for each ministry, the Asahi Shimbun said.

The crackdown comes at the same time as a Health Ministry statement that it would discipline nearly 20 high-level bureaucrats as part of an unfolding scandal that toppled Deputy Health Minister Nobuharu Okamitsu, the daily reported.

Okamitsu resigned and is now facing bribery charges after admitting he took 60 million yen ($526,000) in kickbacks from nursing home developer Hakeshi Koyama, who confessed to giving millions of yen in cash to officials.
The fate of the Health Ministry officials awaiting punishment will be decided on Monday. All took part in lavish parties thrown by Koyama, and accepted invitations to golf at exclusive clubs.
The Yomiuri Shimbun reported the Health Ministry was considering sacking a top-level bureaucrat.

In a concurrent scandal, more than 100 high-ranking Ministry of Trade and Industry (MITI) bureaucrats were being questioned over their links with arrested oil dealer Junichi Izui, who is at the center of an oil industry scandal.

The governor of Akita Prefecture in northern Japan announced last month his imminent resignation, the first by a governor, because of excesses by local bureaucrats involving 900 million yen ($7.9 million) of taxpayers' money.

The announcement came after the resignation of the vice governor of nearby Miyagi Prefecture following revelations of spending on wining and dining totalling about 580 million yen ($5.1 million) by local officials.
